section_summary: This section documents mounting American public, religious, press, and congressional pressure during May–July 1939 to halt exports of arms, scrap iron, petroleum, and other strategic materials to Japan during its war in China. State Department replies explain the limits of the Neutrality Act, report that licensed arms shipments to Japan had effectively ceased, and distinguish those controlled articles from unrestricted commodities. The section also contains Chinese criticism of American trade with Japan, polling data favoring a boycott and embargo, proposed legislation, and extensive lists of organizations protesting assistance to Japan.

subfiles.title: Arthur Capper requests additional copies of the Department's statement on exports to Japan
subfiles.about: Capper asks for twenty-five more copies of a State Department statement concerning exports of war materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Capper thanks Hull for his May 22 letter, finds it suitable for troubled Kansas constituents, and requests more mimeographed copies.

subfiles.title: Reply supplying Capper with twenty-five copies of the export statement
subfiles.about: Hull acknowledges Capper's request and encloses twenty-five copies of the Department's China–Japan export statement.
subfiles.summary: Reply forwards twenty-five copies of the State statement on war-material exports to China and Japan to Capper.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Philip Smead Bird's protest against supplying Japan
subfiles.about: The sheet cross-references a letter protesting U.S. supplies to Japan and enclosing a church resolution.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Philip Smead Bird's protest against supplying Japan and the Church of the Covenant's May 12, 1939 resolution.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to World Peace Foundation statement on an embargo against treaty violators
subfiles.about: The sheet references a World Peace Foundation statement favoring embargoes against Japan or other violators of the Nine-Power Treaty.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to World Peace Foundation's May 10 trustees' opinion on embargoes against violators of the Nine-Power Treaty.

subfiles.title: George A. Dondero forwards a Farmington petition against shipments to Japan
subfiles.about: Dondero forwards a petition from Farmington residents and asks for the Department's position on shipments supporting Japan's war in China.
subfiles.summary: Representative Dondero forwards a Farmington petition against shipments helping Japan's war and requests the Department's current attitude.

subfiles.title: Farmington citizens' petition for a boycott of war-supporting shipments to Japan
subfiles.about: Farmington residents ask Dondero to support an immediate boycott of goods or materials sustaining Japan's war against China.
subfiles.summary: Farmington petition says the US can no longer morally sanction destruction of China and asks a boycott of goods contributing to Japan's war.

subfiles.title: Hull replies to Dondero on exports to China and Japan
subfiles.about: Hull provides the Department's export statement and explains its policy against supplying aircraft used to bomb civilians.
subfiles.summary: Hull sends the statement, recalls the July 1938 moral embargo on aircraft supplies to countries bombing civilians, and says no new Japanese arms licenses were sought or issued for five months.

subfiles.title: D. Lane Powers forwards a petition on traffic in war materials with Japan
subfiles.about: Powers forwards a petition concerning trade in war materials with Japan for State Department consideration.
subfiles.summary: Representative Powers sends a petition on the traffic in war materials with Japan for the Secretary's attention.

subfiles.title: File note describing the petition forwarded by Powers
subfiles.about: The note records that Powers's enclosure was a form petition signed by organizations and individuals.
subfiles.summary: File note: the missing enclosure was a standard-form petition on war-material exports to Japan signed by organizations and individuals.

subfiles.title: Hull replies to Powers and returns the petition
subfiles.about: Hull notes the petition, explains the moral embargo and decline in licensed arms exports to Japan, and returns the enclosure.
subfiles.summary: Hull returns the petition with the Department's export statement, noting no new Japanese arms licenses for five months and older ones expected to lapse.

subfiles.title: Washington Committee for Aid to China transmits a 6,500-signature petition
subfiles.from: Mortimer Graves, Washington Committee for Aid to China
subfiles.about: The committee submits a petition seeking lawful American action against Japanese aggression in China.
subfiles.summary: The committee forwards a petition carrying 6,500 signatures and calling for American action against Japanese aggression under existing law. Although legislative circumstances had changed since the petition was circulated, the committee says the signers still want the State Department to lead in defining an honorable and peace-promoting policy.
keywords: Washington Committee for Aid to China

subfiles.title: Typed copy of the Washington Committee's petition letter
subfiles.from: Mortimer Graves, Washington Committee for Aid to China
subfiles.about: This typed copy reproduces the committee's submission of its 6,500-signature petition.
subfiles.summary: Typed copy of the Washington Committee's appeal for action against Japanese aggression within existing law and State Department guidance toward peace.

subfiles.title: Roster of Washington Committee for Aid to China sponsors
subfiles.from: Washington Committee for Aid to China
subfiles.about: The page lists the committee's religious, civic, political, and professional sponsors.
subfiles.summary: Roster of thirty-four sponsors of the Washington Committee for Aid to China, including clergy, politicians, academics and military figures.
keywords: Washington Committee for Aid to China

subfiles.title: Hull acknowledges the Washington Committee petition
subfiles.about: Hull thanks Graves for the committee's views and returns the petition for possible further use.
subfiles.summary: Hull acknowledges the Washington Committee petition brought by Hornbeck, noting its views and returning it for reuse.

subfiles.title: Internal note recording Welles's refusal to transmit domestic petitions to Congress
subfiles.about: The note records Welles's view that the Department should not serve as a conduit between domestic organizations and Congress.
subfiles.summary: Welles distinguishes Americans in Chengdu, lacking ready access to Congress, from US-based organizations, opposing State transmitting the latter's views to congressional committees.

subfiles.title: Hornbeck routing note requesting consultation with Welles
subfiles.about: Hornbeck asks that his recommendation about the Washington Committee petition be discussed with Welles.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck routing note: extra copies attached; consult Welles on the recommendation on page three.

subfiles.title: Hornbeck memorandum on the Washington Committee petition
subfiles.about: Hornbeck reports receiving the committee's petition and recommends notifying congressional foreign-relations chairmen.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck: Frederick Harris presented Graves's letter and a petition with 6,500 signatures calling for stopping shipments of oil, scrap iron and other materials to Japan; he recommends sending copies to Senate and House committee chairmen.

subfiles.title: J. Will Taylor asks about wartime sales to Japan, Germany, and Italy
subfiles.about: Taylor asks whether U.S. manufacturers may sell Japan anything it can buy and whether the same policy applied to Germany and Italy during the Spanish Civil War.
subfiles.summary: J. Will Taylor asks about current American sales of munitions to Japan, and whether manufacturers could sell freely to Germany and Italy during the Spanish conflict.

subfiles.title: Department reply explaining export law to Taylor
subfiles.about: Hull explains the cessation of licensed arms shipments to Japan and the legal limits of the 1937 neutrality legislation.
subfiles.summary: Hull reports no Japanese arms-export licenses in six months; Germany and Italy faced no arms prohibition since no war finding was made; the 1937 act gave no power over non-arms commodities.

subfiles.title: Mrs. Lorimer questions American Far Eastern and Cuban policy
subfiles.about: Lorimer criticizes the contradiction between protesting Japanese bombing and supplying Japan, and questions U.S. policy in China and Cuba.
subfiles.summary: Mrs. Lorimer notes a British freighter carrying American scrap iron to Japan, questions protecting China investments, invokes the Panay, urges ending dollar diplomacy, and asks why the US allegedly supports Cuban dictatorship.

subfiles.title: Interdivisional routing sheet for the Lorimer correspondence
subfiles.to: Division of Far Eastern Affairs and Division of Controls
subfiles.about: The page routes Lorimer's letter among the State Department divisions responsible for its Far Eastern and Cuban questions.
subfiles.summary: Routing sheet of the Division of the American Republics for the Lorimer correspondence.

subfiles.title: Bonsal memorandum proposing an answer on Cuba
subfiles.about: Bonsal drafts a response denying that the United States supports any particular Cuban regime.
subfiles.summary: Bonsal proposes replying that US-Cuban relations rest on the same sovereign basis as with other governments, so the US does not support a specific Cuban regime.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs memorandum proposing an answer to Lorimer
subfiles.about: The memorandum suggests sending Lorimer earlier official documents explaining U.S. Far Eastern policy.
subfiles.summary: Far Eastern Affairs proposes referring Lorimer to Senate Document No. 131, 1937 press statements and Hull's March 1938 address on Far Eastern policy.

subfiles.title: Haig requests proposed divisional replies to Lorimer's questions
subfiles.from: R. V. Haig, Division of Controls
subfiles.to: Division of Far Eastern Affairs and Division of the American Republics
subfiles.about: Haig asks the responsible divisions to provide suggested answers to Mrs. Lorimer's questions.
subfiles.summary: Haig asks each division whether an answer to Lorimer's multi-division questions is appropriate and what reply it recommends.

subfiles.title: Yost replies to Lorimer on Japan, China, and Cuba
subfiles.about: Yost provides the Department's positions on arms exports, American interests in China, and relations with Cuba.
subfiles.summary: Yost encloses the export statement and describes the moral embargo on aeronautical supplies; no new Japanese arms licenses in five months; rejects the claim that the US supports a particular Cuban regime.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs note summarizing Fuzhou despatch no. 108
subfiles.about: The note flags a Fuzhou newspaper editorial criticizing American responsibility for continuing aggression in China.
subfiles.summary: Far Eastern note: Fuzhou Despatch No. 108's final two paragraphs adequately summarize criticism of the United States.

subfiles.title: Despatch no. 108 on a Fuzhou editorial criticizing the United States
subfiles.from: Alvin T. Rowe Jr., American Consulate, Fuzhou
subfiles.about: Rowe transmits a Chinese editorial holding the United States partly responsible for Japanese aggression because of American arms sales.
subfiles.summary: Vice consul forwards Kuang Kuang-mo's May 13 editorial contrasting Roosevelt's protests with continued American sales to Japan, saying the US shares responsibility for crimes in China.

subfiles.title: Chinese text of “Crimes for Which the United States Should Share the Responsibility”
subfiles.from: Kuang Kuang-mo, Nan Fang Jih Pao
subfiles.about: The Chinese-language editorial condemns the contradiction between American professions of peace and continued material aid to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The editorial cites an appeal from Americans in Chongqing for an embargo following Japanese air raids. It argues that American petroleum, metals, cotton, machinery, and other supplies enable Japanese attacks on China and even on American citizens and property. The writer characterizes U.S. policy as self-defeating and morally inconsistent.

subfiles.title: English translation of “Crimes for Which the United States Should Share the Responsibility”
subfiles.from: Kuang Kuang-mo, Nan Fang Jih Pao
subfiles.about: The translation argues that American trade makes the United States complicit in Japanese aggression and air raids in China.
subfiles.summary: Translated editorial reproduces Chongqing Americans' demand for an embargo, argues continued trade contradicts friendship and justice, and calls US policy complicit and suicidal.

subfiles.title: McCormack forwards Higgins's letter on Japanese aggression
subfiles.about: McCormack forwards a constituent's appeal to stop supplying Japan with war materials and credit.
subfiles.summary: Representative McCormack sends Hull Dudley Higgins's letter on the Sino-Japanese conflict for consideration.

subfiles.title: Higgins urges legislation ending American support for Japan
subfiles.about: Higgins asks McCormack to support legislation stopping war materials and credit from reaching Japan.
subfiles.summary: Higgins says Japan could sustain its China war only briefly without American war materials and credit, urging legislation to end supplies.

subfiles.title: Hull replies to McCormack and returns Higgins's letter
subfiles.about: Hull reports that licensed arms shipments to Japan have ceased and returns the constituent letter.
subfiles.summary: Hull sends the export statement, recalling the moral embargo, and says no Japanese arms licenses were issued in six months and older ones expired, so no arms were shipping.

subfiles.title: Polk forwards “A Suicidal American Policy” and urges international coordination
subfiles.about: Polk forwards C. P. Althaus's editorial and urges investigation and cooperation with Britain and France to restrain Japan.
subfiles.summary: Polk commends Althaus's 'A Suicidal American Policy', cites a Christian Science Monitor editorial naming the US Japan's chief arms provider, and urges exploring an agreement with Britain and France.

subfiles.title: “A Suicidal American Policy”
subfiles.from: C. P. Althaus, The Bethel Journal
subfiles.about: The editorial calls for coordinated American, British, and French economic pressure against Japan.
subfiles.summary: Althaus reviews British-Japanese confrontation and Japanese attacks on American missions, arguing the US supplies resources Japan may use against it and urging coordinated withholding of iron ore, tin, copper and gasoline.

subfiles.title: Hull replies to Polk on the Althaus editorial
subfiles.about: Hull acknowledges the clipping and reports that no arms or implements of war are currently being shipped to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Hull thanks Polk for forwarding Althaus's editorial and encloses the Department's export statement. He recounts the moral embargo on aeronautical supplies to forces bombing civilians. No Japanese arms-export licenses had been issued in six months, and all earlier licenses had expired or been used.

subfiles.title: Capper forwards Southern Baptist boycott and scrap-iron appeal
subfiles.about: Capper forwards Una Roberts Lawrence's letter supporting a Japanese-goods boycott and legislation against scrap-iron exports.
subfiles.summary: Capper forwards a Southern Baptist boycott and scrap-iron appeal, asking whether circumstances changed since Hull last wrote and for a public statement.

subfiles.title: Southern Baptist young women appeal for an embargo and boycott
subfiles.from: Una Roberts Lawrence and Katherine Roberts
subfiles.about: Southern Baptist delegates urge legislation ending war-material exports to Japan and endorse a consumer boycott.
subfiles.summary: Kansas delegation at a Southern Baptist young women's camp, representing 77,143 women, supports a boycott, asks whether scrap-iron exports can end, and requests support for the Schwellenbach bill.

subfiles.title: Hull replies to Capper about the Southern Baptist appeal
subfiles.about: Hull says his earlier export statement remains applicable and supplies updated copies for Capper's use.
subfiles.summary: Hull acknowledges Lawrence's letter and says the information sent to Capper on May 22 remains valid. He sends additional copies of the Department's statement, with current China export figures inserted in one copy. He notes that updated statistics can be obtained from the Division of Controls and returns Lawrence's letter.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of Moffett's inquiry about scrap-iron restrictions
subfiles.from: E. P. Allen, Division of Controls
subfiles.about: Allen records an Iron Age editor's inquiry concerning proposed legislation restricting scrap exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Moffett asks whether Congress may restrict scrap exports; the Japanese ambassador urged buyers to secure scrap before restrictions; he is surprised the 1937 resolution does not authorize the President to ban it.

subfiles.title: Egbert Smith condemns American material support for Japan
subfiles.about: Smith urges Hull to end American support for Japan's war in China.
subfiles.summary: Egbert Smith says American Christians are humiliated that the US is Japan's chief munitions supplier and asks Hull to find a way to end the support.

subfiles.title: Hull replies to Egbert Smith
subfiles.about: Hull acknowledges Smith's protest and refers him to an earlier reply sent to H. Kerr Taylor.
subfiles.summary: Hull assures Smith his views will be considered and refers him to the July 10 letter to H. Kerr Taylor on exports.

subfiles.title: Hope requests information on neutrality and exports to China and Japan
subfiles.about: Hope asks for the State Department's position and export figures so he can answer constituents concerned about the Neutrality Act.
subfiles.summary: Representative Hope asks the Department's position on neutrality and American exports of munitions and war materials to China and Japan.

subfiles.title: Hull replies to Hope on legal controls and Japanese exports
subfiles.about: Hull explains which exports can legally be restricted and reports no Japanese arms licenses during the first half of 1939.
subfiles.summary: Hull explains existing law controls only arms, tinplate scrap and helium; other commodities are freely exportable; compliance with the aeronautical moral embargo and no Japanese arms licenses in six months.

subfiles.title: Price sends Hamilton evidence of American opposition to war-material exports
subfiles.about: Price forwards materials illustrating American public opposition to exports of war supplies to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Price, for the American Committee for Non-Participation, sends Hamilton evidence of public opposition to war-material exports to Japan.

subfiles.title: Fact sheet on U.S. war-material exports and pending Far Eastern bills
subfiles.from: American Committee for Non-Participation in Japanese Aggression
subfiles.about: The sheet quantifies American supplies to Japan and summarizes four proposed measures for restricting trade or credits.
subfiles.summary: Fact sheet: the US supplied about 56 percent of Japan's imported war materials in 1938; summarizes the Pittman and Schwellenbach resolutions and bills by Eaton and Coffee.

subfiles.title: Gallup report on support for a boycott and arms embargo against Japan
subfiles.from: George Gallup, American Institute of Public Opinion
subfiles.to: American Committee for Non-Participation in Japanese Aggression
subfiles.about: The reproduced poll reports sharply increased American sympathy for China and majority support for boycotting Japan and embargoing arms.
subfiles.summary: Gallup poll: sympathy for China rose from 47 to 74 percent, 66 percent back a boycott, and 72 percent favor forbidding arms shipments to Japan versus 40 percent for China.

subfiles.title: Hamilton acknowledges Price's public-opinion materials
subfiles.about: Hamilton thanks Price for providing material on exports of war supplies to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Hamilton acknowledges Price's June 28 letter and enclosed evidence on exports to Japan.

subfiles.title: Price submits Roosevelt a list of organizations protesting aid to Japan
subfiles.about: Price sends Roosevelt a partial list of organizations opposing war-supply sales to Japan and says they represent nearly forty million citizens.
subfiles.summary: Price sends Roosevelt a list of organizations protesting aid to Japan, estimating nearly forty million members, and cites the Gallup poll as showing a growing majority.

subfiles.title: Duplicate Gallup report enclosed with Price's letter to Roosevelt
subfiles.from: George Gallup, American Institute of Public Opinion
subfiles.about: The enclosure reproduces polling data supporting a Japanese-goods boycott and an embargo on arms shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Duplicate Gallup report: growing sympathy for China and majorities for boycotting Japanese goods and banning arms shipments to Japan.

subfiles.title: Partial list of groups protesting aid to Japan or aggressors
subfiles.from: American Committee for Non-Participation in Japanese Aggression
subfiles.about: The enclosure lists national, regional, and local religious, labor, civic, educational, peace, and women's organizations opposing aid to Japan or aggressor states.
subfiles.summary: The six-page compilation identifies national denominations, missionary bodies, labor unions, women's organizations, student groups, peace societies, churches, and local civic bodies that adopted protests or embargo resolutions. It supplies membership or representation figures for many entries and spans communities across the United States. The list documents the geographic and institutional breadth of organized sentiment against shipments to Japan.

subfiles.title: Green acknowledges Price's submission through the White House
subfiles.about: Green acknowledges the list of organizations protesting shipments of war supplies to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Green acknowledges, by White House referral, Price's July 14 letter and thanks him for sending the protest list to the President.

subfiles.title: Cable reporting likely British support for a U.S. embargo on Japan
subfiles.about: The cable reports that Britain is interested in Pittman's bill and would likely follow a congressional embargo on war materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Cable: the European situation makes Britain temporarily patient toward Japan, but it is strongly interested in Pittman's bill and would follow if Congress enacted an embargo.

subfiles.title: Welles asks Hamilton to draft an appropriate reply
subfiles.about: Welles directs Hamilton to prepare a reply to the attached correspondence.
subfiles.summary: Welles asks Hamilton to draft a reply for his signature to the incoming letter.

subfiles.title: Incomplete letter thanking Welles for his stand on American policy
subfiles.about: An unidentified writer thanks Welles for the determined stand he has taken concerning American policy.
subfiles.summary: Incomplete letter thanks Welles for his stand, saying many citizens are aroused that the US is helping Japan; continues beyond this section.
